query: Earlier efforts have produced HfNbTiVAl10 with a hierarchical heterostructure featuring multilevel chemical fluctuations and have used thermophysical-parameter calculations, CALPHAD, first-principles calculations, and machine-learning modeling to identify promising alloys. However, large computational demands and low efficiency impede rapid discovery, while fracture properties such as toughness remain difficult to predict. For HfNbTiVAl10 in its reported hierarchical-heterostructured state, what single testable methodological hypothesis could overcome these limitations for predicting Young’s modulus, yield strength, and toughness under tensile and fracture testing? Explain the rationale, quantify the expected gains in accuracy and efficiency over prior methods, specify the conditions under which it would cease to be reliable, identify supporting prior evidence, and define a blinded prospective benchmark that would decisively falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Integrating a multi‐fidelity surrogate model that combines limited high‐fidelity simulations (e.g., DFT/MD calibrated on hierarchical microstructural features) with machine‐learning algorithms trained on experimentally informed datasets can rapidly and accurately predict the Young’s modulus, yield strength, and toughness of HfNbTiVAl10 in its hierarchical–heterostructured state.
generation.material_initial_state: HfNbTiVAl10 alloy in its reported hierarchical heterostructured state featuring multilevel chemical fluctuations.
generation.intervention: Develop and apply an integrated computational framework in which high‐fidelity simulations of representative microstructural domains are used to generate training data for a machine‐learning surrogate. This surrogate is then employed to predict mechanical responses under tensile and fracture conditions with significantly lower computational demand.
generation.conditions: The methodology is applied under controlled room temperature tensile and fracture testing conditions (with realistic strain rates) that mirror standard experimental protocols. The training data should encompass the range of microstructural variations inherent to the reported hierarchical state.
generation.structural_mediator: The multilevel chemical fluctuations and corresponding local lattice distortions characteristic of the hierarchical heterostructure serve as key mediators linking the microstructural configuration with macroscopic mechanical properties.
generation.mechanism: By using a hybrid approach, the method leverages high-fidelity simulation outputs (e.g., localized bond distortions and phase stability information) to capture the essential physics, while the machine learning model interpolates between these results across the full compositional and microstructural variability. This hierarchy in data fidelity ensures that the dominant deformation mechanisms (elastic, plastic, and fracture-related microstructural rearrangements) are efficiently encoded into rapid predictive algorithms.
generation.predicted_outcome: The approach is expected to yield predictions of Young’s modulus, yield strength, and toughness with improved accuracy (potentially reducing error margins by ~30% relative to standalone CALPHAD/first-principles methods) and with an efficiency gain possibly an order of magnitude faster than conventional high-throughput calculations.
generation.baseline: Prior methods relying exclusively on extensive CALPHAD calculations, first-principles simulations, and high-demand machine-learned models without microstructural mediation.
generation.boundary: The surrogate model may cease to be reliable if the alloy exhibits unforeseen non-linear phase transitions, additional defect-related mechanisms, or extreme microstructural variability that falls outside the range of the training data. Furthermore, if the local chemical fluctuations interact in a manner that is not captured by the selected descriptors, predictive accuracy may degrade.
generation.uncertainty: Exact quantitative improvements in accuracy and efficiency remain uncertain and depend on the quality and representativeness of the high-fidelity training data as well as the selection of appropriate microstructural descriptors. The surrogate’s performance may also be sensitive to unforeseen alloy behavior under extreme testing conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Perform a blinded prospective benchmark wherein a series of HfNbTiVAl10 samples, fabricated to replicate the reported hierarchical heterostructure, are tested under standardized tensile and fracture conditions. The integrated surrogate model’s predictions for Young’s modulus, yield strength, and fracture toughness are recorded prior to testing. A subsequent round of independent mechanical testing (including detailed microstructural characterization) is then performed without knowledge of the predictions.
measurements: Young’s modulus via standardized tensile tests
Toughness measured by fracture and impact testing
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If more than 30% of the experimentally measured properties (across multiple samples and tests) fall outside the 95% confidence interval of the surrogate model predictions, or if systematic deviations are observed that exceed the anticipated error margins (e.g., >30% error increase compared to established baselines), the hypothesis will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Computational investigations of structural, chemical, and deformation behavior in high-entropy alloys (HEAs), which possess notable mechanical strength, have been limited due to the absence of applicable force fields. To extend investigations, we propose a set of intermolecular potential parameters for a quinary Al-Cr-Co-Fe-Ni alloy, using the available ternary Embedded Atom Method and Lennard-Jones potential in classical molecular-dynamics simulations. The simulation results are validated by a comparison to first-principles Korringa-Kohn-Rostoker (KKR) - Coherent Potential Approximation (CPA) [KKR-CPA] calculations for the HEA structural properties (lattice constants and bulk moduli), relative stability, pair probabilities, and high-temperature short-range ordering. The simulation (MD)-derived properties are in quantitative agreement with KKR-CPA calculations (first-principles) and experiments. We study Al x CrCoFeNi for Al ranging from 0 ≤ x ≤2 mole fractions, and find that the HEA shows large chemical clustering over a wide temperature range for x < 0.5. Unlike other conventional alloys based on a “principal element,” high-entropy alloy (HEA) is a unique material that maintains a random solid solution structure without forming intermetallic compounds in operating temperatures due to its high configurational entropy [1] – [3] . It also has outstanding physical and chemical properties, which makes it a potential replacement for traditional metallic materials, and it has recently been referred to as a multi-principal element alloy (MPEA) or compositionally concentrated alloy (CCA) [4] – [9] .

As attention in HEAs increases, many studies have been conducted to explore its mechanical, physical and chemical properties [10] – [15] . In particular, equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi HEA, which was the first developed HEA, is the most studied because of its excellent combination of tensile strength and elongation along with excellent fracture toughness and corrosion resistance [6] , [16] – [21] . However, despite the advantages of equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi HEA, many issues arise owing to its low yield strength and costly and complex thermomechanical processing (i.e., multiple casting → hot rolling → homogenization → cold rolling → annealing → cutting, etc.

The concept of HEAs provides us an unprecedented degree of freedom in the design of advanced alloys with promising properties. For the rapid exploration of the vast compositional space and investigation of the composition and temperature effects on the microstructure, advanced HEA-design strategies and efficient tools are necessary. At present, a few advanced HEA-design strategies were reported by combining the physicochemical criteria, CALPHAD, data mining, and multi-objective optimization algorithm [21] , [22] , [35] – [37] , demonstrating that the CALPHAD method has played an important role in the design of advanced HEAs. There are two essential requirements to carry out calculations, using the CALPHAD method: computational software and database.

The computational software could significantly affect the efficiency of HTC since massive calculations are carried out. In the example of the Al–Cr–Fe–Mn–Ti quinary system, it takes only a few hours on a desktop computer to finish the HTCs (~ 3 × 10 3 ) within the composition range of 5–50 at.% for each element and finally screen out eight potential alloys.
